chapters.title: The Greatest Builders in the Ancient World

pages.text: When people think of Egypt, they think of pyramids. The pyramids of Egypt are among the most famous structures ever built. They have stood for thousands of years in the desert on the west bank of the River Nile. They are so large, so precise, and so old that people have been trying to understand them ever since.

image.note: Illustration: The Giza plateau with the three great pyramids and the Sphinx against a desert sky

pages.text: The largest pyramid in the world is the Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE. It is made from approximately 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite. Some of those blocks weigh more than eighty tonnes each. The pyramid stands 138 metres tall. For nearly four thousand years, it was the tallest structure on earth.

Egypt was one of the great civilisations of the ancient world. For more than three thousand years, it was ruled by pharaohs, god-kings who governed the land, commanded vast armies, and controlled enormous wealth. The pharaohs believed that their power continued after death, and they built their tombs accordingly: monuments so vast and permanent that they would last forever.

The pyramids were those tombs. Inside each pyramid was a burial chamber, designed to protect the pharaoh's body and preserve everything he or she would need in the afterlife: treasures, food, weapons, furniture, and servants represented in art on the walls. The pyramid's purpose was to ensure that the pharaoh's power and identity survived death.

image.note: Cross-section diagram of a pyramid showing burial chamber, passages, and outer casing

pages.text: The ancient Egyptians believed in a complex afterlife. When a pharaoh died, their body was preserved through a process called mummification, wrapped in linen bandages, and placed in a series of decorated coffins. The spirit, they believed, needed the body to return to after travelling through the underworld. Losing the body meant losing the afterlife.

The pyramid protected the body. Its massive weight and the complexity of its internal passages were designed to prevent tomb robbers from reaching the burial chamber. Despite these precautions, most Egyptian pyramids were eventually robbed, some in ancient times, some much later. The treasures inside them are now, for the most part, gone. The bodies of the pharaohs were moved by priests to hidden locations to protect them.
Cross-reference: How were the Egyptian pyramids built? See Chapter Two.

Mummification took seventy days. First the internal organs were removed and preserved in special containers called canopic jars. The heart alone was left in place, because the Egyptians believed it would be weighed in the afterlife against the feather of truth. The body was dried using a salt called natron, rubbed with oils and resins, and wrapped in hundreds of metres of linen bandages. Amulets were tucked between the layers to protect the pharaoh on the journey ahead.

Guarding the Giza plateau is the Great Sphinx, a colossal statue with the body of a lion and the head of a pharaoh, carved from a single ridge of limestone. It is 73 metres long and 20 metres high. Its nose is famously missing, broken off centuries ago. The Sphinx faces the rising sun, and most archaeologists believe it was carved during the reign of the pharaoh Khafre, whose pyramid stands directly behind it.

The Egyptian pyramids were built without any of the machines that modern engineers rely on: no cranes, no steel cables, no motorised vehicles. Every block was quarried by hand, transported by human and animal labour, and lifted into position by workers using ramps, sledges, and rope.

The limestone blocks used in the Great Pyramid came mostly from a quarry nearby. The granite used for the burial chamber came from Aswan, nearly 800 kilometres to the south. Moving those granite blocks down the River Nile on rafts and then across the desert to Giza was one of the great logistical achievements of the ancient world.

image.note: Map of Egypt showing Giza, Aswan, and the Nile with arrows indicating transport routes

pages.text: For a long time, people assumed that the pyramids were built by slaves, possibly prisoners captured in war. Recent archaeological evidence suggests this is wrong. The workers who built the pyramids were Egyptian citizens, paid in food, clothing, and medical care. They lived in a purpose-built workers' village near the pyramid site. The village has been excavated and provides remarkable evidence of how they lived.

The workers were organised into teams and crews, each with a name and an identity. Records found at the site show rosters, work schedules, and accounts of rations. This was not a chaotic mob of forced labourers. It was a highly organised workforce, directed by skilled engineers and administrators who planned every aspect of construction in extraordinary detail.

The ramps used to move the blocks upward are still debated among archaeologists. No ramp has ever been found intact, but evidence of different ramp designs has been identified at various pyramid sites. Some researchers believe a straight ramp was used; others argue for a spiral ramp that wound around the pyramid as it rose. The question has not yet been settled.

What is beyond doubt is the precision of the finished structure. The base of the Great Pyramid is almost perfectly square, with each side measuring approximately 230 metres and differing from each other by less than eight centimetres. The four sides are oriented almost exactly to the four points of the compass. This level of accuracy, achieved without modern instruments, is extraordinary.
Cross-reference: What is inside the pyramids? See Chapter Three.

None of this building would have been possible without the River Nile. Every year the river flooded, covering the fields with rich black silt and making Egyptian farmland among the most productive in the ancient world. The flood season was also the building season. While the fields lay underwater, farmers could not farm, and many joined the pyramid workforce instead. The Nile fed the workers, carried the stone, and set the rhythm of the whole project.

The workers ate surprisingly well. Excavations at the workers' village have uncovered bakeries that produced thousands of loaves of bread a day, and enormous quantities of cattle, sheep, and goat bones. Meat was expensive in ancient Egypt, yet the pyramid builders ate it regularly. Their skeletons show healed fractures that received proper medical care. Whatever else the pyramids were, they were not built by starving slaves. The evidence is in the rubbish heaps.

The interior of the Great Pyramid is not simply a hollow chamber. It is a series of passages and rooms connected in a complex arrangement that archaeologists have been mapping and studying for centuries.

image.note: Cross-section of Great Pyramid showing King's Chamber, Queen's Chamber, Grand Gallery, and entrance passages

pages.text: The most important room is the King's Chamber, located at the heart of the pyramid. It is built entirely from red granite. The ceiling consists of nine enormous granite slabs, each weighing approximately fifty tonnes, resting on the chamber walls. Above the ceiling are five further chambers, designed to distribute the enormous weight of the pyramid above without crushing the burial room below.

Leading to the King's Chamber is the Grand Gallery, a corridor nearly nine metres high and almost fifty metres long, with walls that lean inward as they rise, meeting in a narrow ceiling. The function of the Grand Gallery is still not fully understood, but it is one of the most impressive spaces ever created in the ancient world.

When Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in the Valley of the Kings in 1922, it was the first royal Egyptian burial to be found largely intact. The treasures inside, including Tutankhamun's golden death mask, are now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. The pyramids themselves had been robbed long before any modern archaeologist arrived, but Tutankhamun's tomb, hidden and forgotten for three thousand years, gave the world its clearest picture of what a royal Egyptian burial looked like.

The walls of Egyptian tombs and temples were covered with hieroglyphics, the ancient Egyptian writing system, and with detailed paintings showing scenes from the pharaoh's life, battles, rituals, and the journey through the afterlife. These images and texts are the primary source of everything we know about ancient Egyptian belief and culture.

image.note: Illustration: Detail of Egyptian hieroglyphic wall carvings with labels identifying common symbols

pages.text: Cross-reference: What happened to the pharaohs and their civilisation? See Chapter Four.

For centuries, nobody could read hieroglyphics. The knowledge had been completely lost. Then, in 1799, French soldiers in Egypt discovered a slab of stone at a town called Rosetta. The same message was carved on it three times: once in hieroglyphics, once in a later Egyptian script, and once in ancient Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, the Rosetta Stone became the key that unlocked the entire written history of ancient Egypt.

The scholar who finally cracked the code was a young Frenchman named Jean-Francois Champollion. In 1822, after years of obsessive work, he proved that hieroglyphs recorded the sounds of the Egyptian language, not just pictures of ideas. When the breakthrough came, he reportedly ran to his brother's office, shouted that he had done it, and fainted. Thanks to him, the voices of people who lived four thousand years ago can be read today.

The ancient Egyptian civilisation lasted for more than three thousand years, from around 3100 BCE to 30 BCE, when Egypt became part of the Roman Empire. In that time, Egypt was ruled by thirty dynasties of pharaohs, built thousands of temples and monuments, and created one of the richest and most complex cultures the world has ever seen.

Ancient Egypt was not one unchanging thing. It passed through periods of great power and periods of weakness, was invaded by foreign rulers, recovered, expanded, and contracted again. The pyramids were built during one of Egypt's most powerful periods, known as the Old Kingdom, roughly from 2686 to 2181 BCE. After that, pharaohs were buried in tombs cut into rock rather than in pyramids.

Today, the pyramids of Giza are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited places on earth. The Great Pyramid is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. Every year, millions of people travel to Egypt to see them. They are a central part of Egypt's national identity and a major source of the country's income from tourism.

image.note: Photograph-style illustration of tourists at the base of the Great Pyramid showing its vast scale

pages.text: Archaeologists are still making discoveries at Giza and at other Egyptian sites. In 2023, a tunnel was found beneath the temple of Taposiris Magna, near Alexandria, that some researchers believe may lead to the tomb of Cleopatra, the last pharaoh of ancient Egypt. The pyramids may be the most studied monuments in human history, but they have not yet given up all of their secrets.

The pyramids of Egypt and the pyramids of Nsude in Nigeria were built by different peoples, in different times, from different materials, for different purposes. What connects them is the human impulse that produced both: the decision to build something that reaches upward, something that gives a sacred purpose a permanent physical form. That impulse appears in cultures all over the world. It is, perhaps, one of the most deeply human things there is.

Egypt is not the only African country with pyramids. South of Egypt, in what is now Sudan, the ancient kingdom of Kush built more than two hundred pyramids at sites such as Meroe. They are steeper and smaller than the Egyptian pyramids, and they were built later, but there are actually more pyramids standing in Sudan today than in Egypt. Africa's pyramid story stretches along the whole length of the Nile, and, as this series shows, far beyond it.
